section.title: Rahul Pandey: Startup to Pinterest, Meta Staff, TLM, and Founding Taro
section.deck: Rahul Pandey traces a path from a Stanford spin-out to Pinterest, Meta staff engineer, tech lead manager and startup founder, arguing that credentials, mentors, clear stories and relationships compound while luck can be partly manufactured.

blocks.text: Rahul Pandey is a software engineer who went from a Stanford spin-out startup to Pinterest, then to Meta, where he reached staff level (IC6) and later a tech-lead-manager (TLM) role, before leaving to co-found Taro. He walks the host, Ryan, through that path in order. In Rahul's account, early credentials made risk cheap, and promotions came from mentorship, self-built tooling, clearly framed stories and trust built over time. Management and founding suit people who enjoy helping others and hold strong opinions. Much of the outcome, he says, was luck, which can be partly manufactured by staying curious about people and sharing work. Everything below is Rahul's recollection and opinion unless marked as Ryan's.
blocks.heading: Rahul Pandey's view: use credentials to take bets, build things, and let relationships compound

blocks.title: Career stages (editorial summary of Rahul's account)
rows: Took a bet on a professor's startup while holding multiple big-tech offers; acquired by Pinterest within about eight months of formation.
L3, then L4 after two rejections and an appeal
Moved from recommendation systems to Android; a staff-level mentor and pair programming; a promotion packet that needed clearer framing.
Led a migration of Portal's calling infrastructure back onto Messenger's, plus a self-started debug tool for Portal engineers.
A hybrid role Rahul found taxing and unsustainable long term; he switched teams, then left.
Left with a trusted co-founder, financial runway and an audience built through tutorials and webinars; went through Y Combinator.

blocks.question: Why did Rahul join a very small startup straight out of Stanford?
answer: Rahul stayed a fifth year at Stanford, finishing an undergraduate and a master's degree, partly because he felt he had made no faculty connections. He worked as a research assistant in the lab of a rising-star professor, who later spun the lab's work out into a company. Rahul notes that Stanford is generous about letting faculty start companies.

He had offers from Google, Microsoft and Meta, and he knew he could be one of 10,000 or 20,000 engineers in big tech. The startup offered mutual trust with the professor and a distinctly Silicon Valley story: great if it went well, a good story if not. Aside from the two founders (the professor and an industry veteran), Rahul counts himself as roughly employee number two. Ryan adds that so early in a career there was little responsibility to lose.

followups.question: How did Rahul think about the risk compared with a safer big-tech job?
answer: Rahul gives two reasons. First, he sees most early career moves as two-way doors: try it, learn, and go to big tech later if needed. Second, he would probably not have taken the risk without prior approval from big tech. After a 2013 Facebook internship he received five offers (Google, Facebook, Microsoft, Twitter and Square), which with Stanford on his resume he calls an insurance policy.
Without it, he says, he would have thought twice and taken a stable job first, so that his second job would be easier to land.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: Was the startup's acquisition a strong outcome, or closer to an acqui-hire?
answer: Closer to an acqui-hire, Rahul says. He calls "acquisition" one of the most overloaded terms in Silicon Valley. At one end is a deal such as WhatsApp's sale to Facebook in 2014, which Rahul puts at 19 billion dollars. At the other end is a failed company whose sale is called an acquisition to protect the founders' dignity. His startup sat in the middle, nearer the failure end, though he hesitates to call it a failure.

He describes it as an opportunistic bet. The company had interesting, fairly academic intellectual property but no clear route to revenue or a product. Pinterest, already a hot company with 100 million users, offered to pair that technology with its product-market fit. The startup ended within about eight months of formation. Rahul says the package was somewhat higher than a normal Pinterest new grad's, not life-changing money.

He adds that storytelling is powerful: the story of an enterprising 22-year-old taking a bet on a startup has given him a lot of mileage. When mentoring, he says that if two options are close, the one with more unique people, opportunities and stories is a good one to pick.
blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: Would Rahul recommend the same startup choice to a new grad today?
answer: It depends, Rahul says, and he treats his own case as the exception. It made sense for him because he already had social proof (Stanford and a Facebook internship). The founder was also, in his view, among the best in the world on recommendation systems and big data, so he could learn from watching that person. With those conditions he would encourage a risky bet.

For the typical new grad, with a decent school and a degree but trouble finding a first job, he recommends the biggest reputable brand available, such as Amazon or Google. He argues that credibility accrues there and sets up whatever comes next, and that the standard path is standard for a reason.

Ryan agrees. In Ryan's view, a big-brand job gives an instant step change in credibility, and one or two years at big tech to build engineering fundamentals while collecting that stamp is one of the highest expected-value moves.
blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: What was it like to be acquired by Pinterest?
answer: Rahul says he was happy in the end, but the process was chaotic and stressful. The two founders had 20 years or more of experience and were better informed. One day the team was told that Pinterest would acquire the company and interview everyone, with a full round the following Monday, only a couple of days away.

Rahul had been out of interview prep for almost a year, and he stresses that interview prep is a different skill from engineering work. Pinterest took the whole team straight to a final round: five or six interviews in one day. Rahul was borderline and was called back to the San Francisco office for two more interviews, which he says he did well, and then he got the offer.

The stakes were real, he says. A Tech Crunch article announced the deal, and the company was only about eight months old, so nothing had vested; failing would have meant no equity upside. After the on-site he messaged old recruiters at other big-tech companies as a backup, though he still wanted to join Pinterest with the people he knew.

followups.question: Was the Pinterest interview loop a standard algorithm loop?
answer: Rahul says it was standard: LeetCode-style coding, questions about his startup projects, and one behavioral interview. Ryan notes that failing it would have made for a much weaker story.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: How was Rahul leveled at Pinterest, and how did he choose a team?
answer: Pinterest had just created a leveling system, borrowed from Google and Facebook. Rahul came in at L3, the entry level (L4 is mid-level and L5 senior). He moved away from recommendation systems and data engineering into mobile, which he calls a career reset. It meant a longer ramp-up and, later, a rejected promotion.

Pinterest let new hires choose a team through "base camp," a two-to-three-week version of Facebook's boot camp. Rahul decided against backend work. He wanted to be close to the product and able to build things end to end, including side projects, and liked the idea of an app in the Android store that his Android-using family could try. His startup had no mobile team, so he saw Pinterest as a chance to learn Android professionally with strong people and benefit twice, at work and on the side.

followups.question: Did Rahul learn what he wanted to learn on the Android team?
answer: Yes, though the first months were rough. A strong staff-level engineer joined a couple of months after Rahul, and the mentorship was a huge pivot. But Rahul says he had not yet learned how to learn. The Android app already had hundreds of thousands of lines of code. He read documentation and code but wrote little of his own, and he links that slow ramp-up to his first failed promotion.

What changed, he says, was being surrounded by good people, especially an L6 engineer from Facebook who started pair programming with him. Being accountable to a team that would judge his work was a fire under him. With mentorship and enough time in the role, it eventually clicked.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

followups.question: What matters most when picking a team?
answer: Rahul names two things. The first is the people, because what he learns is dominated by who he interacts with. The second is how important the team is to the company. In 2015 Pinterest's big initiative was international growth, and Android dominates outside the US, so he expected the company to put smart people and money behind it. His view is that working adjacent to an area of high growth means seeing some of that growth yourself.

Ryan relates this to the idea that a rising tide lifts all boats. Ryan has seen people go from new grad to director in five years by working on the company's most important problem and delivering, since career growth tends to track impact.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: How did Rahul eventually get promoted after the failed promotion at Pinterest?
answer: Rahul calls it a difficult journey. The first rejection came about a year after he joined. He thinks the feedback was fair: he had done Android professionally for only about nine months and had not shipped much. He tried again six months later and was rejected again, which he found truly demoralizing. He had arrived through an acqui-hire expecting to be among the best engineers, and two rejections for the same promotion were a real setback.

Pinterest had an appeal process, and Rahul worked with his manager to use it. The appeal succeeded. The anonymous committee had read one project in his packet, described as 16 months of work, as a lack of urgency. Rahul says that was not true. His manager clarified and advocated for him. His lesson is to be clear about what a document says, because readers may interpret it differently, and to have promotion and one-on-one documents reviewed by experienced people.

Ryan notes that a long project can instead signal larger scope. Rahul agrees that context decides: align with the manager on the narrative and collect feedback from tech leads, because 16 months can look impressive, or count against you if it was a minor experiment others expect to take three months. His conclusion is not to assume how others will judge you. Software engineering is a social endeavor, so learn your evaluators' view of your growth areas before a review.

followups.question: What helped Rahul build skills quickly from L3 to L4?
answer: Rahul credits a lesson from the mentor: be willing to work outside the main codebase. Building the Android app and deploying it to a phone sometimes took two to five minutes, so debugging was slow. The mentor showed Rahul how to create a small separate Android app, copy over themes, and iterate in that sandbox with a much faster loop.

Making a new app had seemed like a big, ambiguous task, but it was easy and raised his speed. It also removed his fear of breaking things and copy-pasting code, which helped with side projects. He calls this the biggest mindset shift behind the L3 to L4 promotion. Ryan agrees that a fast iteration loop matters when promotion rests on contributing more code.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: Why did Rahul leave Pinterest for Meta in mid-2017?
answer: Rahul gives three reasons: Meta was a much bigger company with a stronger engineering brand, it paid more, and he did not see a clear path to rapid growth at Pinterest. He wanted to see whether he could get a meaningful bump in level or compensation.

He thinks job hopping works better early in a career than later. As people move up, he says, impact comes mostly through influence. A staff or principal engineer rarely writes enough code to justify the role; they build frameworks, tools and systems that make other developers productive, which takes years of relationships and trust. Early on, showing you can write high-quality production code may be enough to be hired higher.
Ryan's experience matches. Ryan's move from senior to staff was unusually quick because of long relationships on one team, while peers who switched companies quickly had fewer such ties.

followups.question: Was another prestigious name on the resume the real reason?
answer: Partly, Rahul says. He admits some ego in wanting a brand everyone had heard of, since far more people knew Facebook than Pinterest. But he agrees it was not the main factor: he already had Facebook and other known names on his resume. The main reason was a sense that he could grow his career much faster at Facebook.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: What cultural and technical differences did Rahul notice between Pinterest and Meta?
answer: Culturally, Rahul found them similar, since Pinterest's culture was shaped by ex-Facebook and ex-Google people. He describes Facebook as the authentic version, "on steroids." At Pinterest, every change needed at least two reviewers, and Herald rules added blocking reviewers automatically. At Facebook one accept was usually enough to land code, which shocked him.

He also found people more direct at Facebook. At Pinterest, he says, a common criticism was that the company was too nice: people avoided hard feedback or prioritization, so projects and people who should not have stayed lingered. At Facebook people more readily said a project made no sense and should be cut, and he perceived a more aggressive performance-improvement-plan culture.

followups.question: Was learning Meta's custom stack difficult?
answer: On paper the stacks were similar: Android with Java, and no Kotlin yet. Facebook's scale meant many workarounds and a custom build system, Buck, which Rahul found easy. The harder part was that he joined Portal, then called Building 8, a hardware team. Its software was a forked Android with about 30 custom Android apps on a custom operating system, so its build system and tooling differed even from the rest of Facebook. It took him roughly four or five months to understand it.

Ryan explains that Portal is a standalone video-calling device. Rahul adds that the team first used an Android tablet, later flashing custom hardware with their own OS. Building all 30 apps would take three or four hours, so each engineer built only their own app, in Rahul's case the calling app.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

followups.question: What did the debug tool Rahul built for Portal achieve?
answer: Because the Portal workflow was so unusual, Rahul came to understand how it differed from other engineers' and built a debug tool for people on Portal. He says hundreds of engineers in the Portal org or nearby orgs used it daily or weekly, and estimates it saved hundreds of hours of engineering time each month. Ryan says this sounds like IC6-level impact.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: Was Rahul hired at IC5, and did he have to do anything special for that jump?
answer: Rahul was hired at IC5 (senior), so the move from Pinterest was effectively a promotion. He did nothing special, he says; the level was Meta's proposal after interviews in which he felt he had solved nearly every problem.

He also came from a position of strength: a couple of pending offers, a Facebook internship, time at a respectable company, and a hot market for Android developers, all of which made Meta want to give him a compelling offer.
blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: What work led to the promotion from senior to staff (IC6)?
answer: Rahul worked on Portal. Facebook already had a mature cross-platform video-calling infrastructure inside Messenger. Portal's first step was to fork Messenger and go its own way as an experiment. Once Portal had hundreds of thousands of daily users, the team needed to return to the normal infrastructure, because the Messenger RTC team kept improving it. Rahul's main project was migrating Portal's core infrastructure back to Messenger's, keeping Portal's custom features and adopting the new capabilities RTC offered.

He calls it cross-functional work with a lot of bureaucracy, involving the Messenger team, Portal leadership and product managers. Some people can rely on one big project at staff level, he says, but a portfolio worked well for him. The second project was the debug tool, purely engineering-driven and built for himself and his teammates. Together, he says, the two made a clear promotion case.

followups.question: Was Rahul intentional about reaching IC6?
answer: Rahul says how the promotion conversation is phrased matters. In his first year at Facebook the goal was to do well. Later, as a manager, he learned that a new hire who immediately asks for help getting promoted is a turn-off. He also felt imposter syndrome from joining at a fairly high level, so he focused on meeting or exceeding IC5 expectations first.

After about a year, with some trust built and good work landed, he had a clear conversation with his manager about growing on the IC ladder. Since he enjoyed talking to and mentoring people, they also discussed management. They agreed, and Rahul thinks it was the right call, that he should climb the IC ladder first and try management later.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

followups.question: Did Rahul create the scope for the shared-infrastructure project, or was it assigned?
answer: Neither, exactly. Rahul says it was obvious that someone had to do it, and both the RTC team and the Portal team wanted it. The open question was who would be point person. With long tenure, seniority and a relationship with the Messenger RTC team, he was a natural fit, and he says it was clear to everyone that he was one of the best people, perhaps the best, to take it on.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: Why did Rahul move from IC6 to tech lead manager (TLM)?
answer: Rahul says his current company is about helping people, and he sees good managers as people with a real desire to help others grow. As a byproduct, he says, they can have large impact, since managers are usually senior and respected. He also had context and relationships, so the move felt natural: a growing team needed someone to give feedback and keep people on high-impact work, and he had already expressed interest.

followups.question: What concrete steps should someone take if they want to try management?
answer: Rahul starts with a question: do you enjoy helping and working with people? If you dread one-on-ones, he says, you will struggle, because management is mostly one-on-ones and reacting to pings, so a manager cannot guard their time. He suggests testing this by actually holding one-on-ones and leading meetings now.

His second point is having opinions: about the quality of the team's work, and about how the team and organization should change as priorities shift. He thinks the best managers have a strong point of view and bend the organization toward it. Ryan suggests tech-leadership and direction-setting work is a good simulation, and Rahul agrees: very senior ICs must also articulate and sell clear opinions about what the team should do over the next six months or year. Someone who would rather just execute and write code is not a good fit for management.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

followups.question: What surprised Rahul about management, and what did he learn about the TLM role?
answer: Rahul found the TLM role tougher and more taxing than expected. Straddling IC and management work meant that at the end of a day he asked what he had actually achieved, since his time went to meetings, one-on-ones and roadmapping.

He thinks TLM is fine as a transitional role while deciding between full-time management and full-time IC, but not sustainable long term. It is unclear whether you are judged on code or on people leadership. He switched teams afterward. Ryan, who also became a TLM, asked many TLMs beforehand and says every one advised against staying long term, because the role makes you a jack of all trades and master of none.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: Why did Rahul leave Meta to start his own company?
answer: Rahul says the idea of starting a company had been in his mind since around 2016; it was a question of when. He lists three reasons it felt right at Meta. The biggest was a co-founder he trusted, enjoyed working with, and whose timeline matched his. Second, he felt he had reached a satisfying level, or in a more negative framing had plateaued, with a harder path to director. Third, pay, promotions and stock growth meant he did not need to work for a few years.
He also had a signal: Android tutorials he had published on YouTube since 2019. He enjoyed teaching and working with developers and wanted to see whether he could build on it.

followups.question: Where did Rahul find his co-founder?
answer: The co-founder is Alex. They worked together on Portal in 2017, when Alex was on the same team for a few months, and stayed in touch after Alex moved to Instagram. Before COVID they met weekly in person at Facebook. After COVID began they talked almost every other day about ideas to try together.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

followups.question: Had they built anything before quitting?
answer: Nothing was built. They had committed to each other to work on it for at least six months or a year, and they knew the broad domain, career growth. For roughly six months before quitting they did community building and research, running free webinars on career growth during COVID. Rahul says one drew around 800 people, partly because people wanted social interaction at home. They planned to look for funding or build something after quitting.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: Is Y Combinator the best way for a big-tech employee to start a company?
answer: It depends, Rahul says, because "start a company" is as overloaded a term as acquisition. It might mean utility Android apps, small apps earning about 5,000 dollars a month, or a billion-dollar company. For those aiming at the largest outcomes, YC makes sense as a funding vehicle, depending on one's network.

A first-time founder without much of a network should find YC a no-brainer, he says: credibility, money and accountability. A repeat founder, or someone who already knows top-tier VC firms, can argue that YC is not worth it.
blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: What are the biggest differences between running a startup and working in big tech?
answer: Rahul names structure and accountability first. At a three-person company there is no boss and no deadline, whereas Facebook or Pinterest has a cadence of quarterly releases and launches. The founders try to manufacture urgency. He finds this both empowering and scary, because without urgency a team could spend five years twiddling its thumbs.

The second difference is ambiguity about what to build. Taro began as a developer tool, perhaps for reviewing or writing code. The team found the community angle more powerful, which led to courses and then to a fairly robust course platform. He says big-tech engineers often lack product-management skills such as talking to users, iterating on feedback and reading data, and a tiny company has no data scientist or user researcher next to you.
blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: At what point does it make sense to start a company?
answer: Rahul says it depends on how you define success. In his view, climbing to director or higher at Meta gives an amazing life, in the top 0.1 percent of people in the world. But more control and autonomy plus an outlier outcome, meaning a small chance of a huge result, is hard inside big tech. He doubts Meta will grow five or ten times in value in five years, while admitting he could be wrong.

His rule of thumb is to go for a bigger swing once you have stability: big-tech credibility and finances. The other ingredient is a co-founder you get along with, which he compares to a marriage. Timing is the other trap: some people wait for the dream co-founder who is never on the same timeline, because of bonuses or vesting, children, or marriage. Aligned timelines and commitment on how long to run the startup matter as much as the person.
Ryan adds a friend who left Meta to start a company and said they would regret reaching the end of a standard big-tech career without a story worth telling.
blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: In which period did Rahul feel the most skill or career growth?
answer: Rahul names three. The first was meeting the mentor at Pinterest: pair programming, learning by osmosis, and discovering he was empowered to change his environment. The second was at Meta, leading the migration and building the debug tool, which was the first time in big tech he felt he created value, from an idea of his own that people chose to adopt. Before that he often felt like a worker bee carrying out work passed down from above. He says this helped give him the confidence to start a company.

The third, less relevant to a big-tech audience, was the two or three months of Y Combinator: weekly group check-ins brought intense pressure, since underperformers were effectively shamed, and he learned a lot.
blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: Does Rahul have regrets?
answer: His main candidate is the 2014 startup. He does not exactly regret it, since he learned a lot and has a good story. But he suspects the choice was somewhat ego-driven: he did not want to be one of many people in big tech and wanted something unique. He doubts he had enough engineering maturity for it and says he floundered a bit at the startup and at first at Pinterest. A more structured environment might have been the better bet.

Otherwise he has few regrets and feels lucky. He says he was rejected from jobs he would have taken, at companies that he says "completely exploded" a year later, and he counts that as luck. A few venture firms also strung Taro along with promised valuations, then declined, and he now believes those investors' pressure on the cap table would have been bad for the company.
blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: How much of Rahul's career growth was luck?
answer: Rahul says he feels he has "failed my way into success" and that a lot of it was luck, in the opportunities and people he came across. He adds that luck can be manufactured by being curious about the people and opportunities around you. Finding his co-founder, the 2014 startup and the Facebook opportunities all came from keeping in touch: asking what someone is up to, what they like about a new job, or offering help on a project.

He says the debug tool came from talking to people about their workflows, and many job hops came from knowing what respected people were doing. He sees this as a repeatable process, not luck. He also describes posting on social media as deliberate: people who see helpful content think of you for opportunities.

Ryan notes that some people call this maximizing your luck surface area, and says internal writing and reaching out give the same visibility at a company. Ryan suggests that credibility from such sharing probably helped Rahul get the shared-infrastructure project that led to staff.

followups.question: How can someone network without it feeling manufactured?
answer: Rahul hesitates to call what he does networking. He points to two ingredients: genuine curiosity about what the other person is doing, and thoughtfulness about what he shares. Rather than only asking questions or for mentorship, he says one of the best ways to build a relationship is to share something he has worked on that may interest the other person.

In his words, showcasing what you are up to creates gravity: people are drawn to you for your opinion, so it becomes a two-way street. If you always ask and it is never reciprocated, the other person may simply not be interested, or you may need to become more interesting.
Ryan recalls that networking felt artificial as a new grad, but side projects such as writing content and building a keyboard make conversations natural.
followups.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey

blocks.question: What advice would Rahul give his college-graduate self?
answer: Rahul wishes he had realized much earlier that there are no gatekeepers: you need no permission to learn a technology or try something new. He did well in school by being methodical and studious, but not as creative or exploratory as he could have been. He admires Ryan's keyboard project as something nobody told Ryan to do. He cites his own recent projects, such as extensions for a Mac app launcher, as the kind of work he means.

In his view, feeling empowered to do something unique based on what you care about, rather than what peers, instructors or managers expect, is how you get an outlier outcome. He wishes he had cultivated creative interests earlier and set aside time for them deliberately.

Ryan observes that Rahul took more initiative later. Rahul agrees: YouTube tutorials, published Android apps and webinars with 800 people felt like a blindfold lifting. His advice is not to wait until you are ready to start a company, publish an app or teach, but to do it now. He was passive early on, waiting to get better and smarter, and wishes he had adopted that mindset in middle or high school.

Ryan frames this as main-character energy versus NPC energy. Rahul likes the framing but adds that you need not be the main character in every domain. It is enough to do so in the parts of life you care about or where you have a unique take.
blocks.speaker: Rahul Pandey
